name: Elena Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior cook at Hearth and Grain, a busy brunch and lunch restaurant with a big wood oven in the middle of the room. I'm in at half six to fire the oven, then I'm on eggs, toast and the brunch plates until two, and I help with the bread when Chef Agnes lets me. Agnes is sixty and has been baking forty years. My loaves still come out flat half the time, but she's patient.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the bread, the smell at seven in the morning, it's like my grandmother's kitchen. The weekend brunch queue wears me out, two hours of eggs nonstop. My boyfriend Mateo is an apprentice plumber, and we're saving to get married, about three months of money between us. One day I want my own little bakery, that's the dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, some things should stay the way they are. Bread is made by hands. I'd say that at church and people would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried about Hearth and Grain. The lease comes up next year, and the owner said the landlord wants a lot more. If the rent goes up too much, the place could close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning bread from Agnes, every morning I can. Save hard for the wedding and the bakery, maybe sell loaves at the Saturday market. I use AI now and then to work out the cost of a loaf, so I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A little worry about the lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if Hearth and Grain closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find another brunch kitchen, there are a few in town. But I'd lose Agnes, and that's the part I'd mind. You can't learn bread from a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you think the market stall could bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe forty or fifty loaves a Saturday, if they come out right. It's not much, but it's a start. And it tells me if people would buy my bread.

say: Some things should **stay** the way they are, and bread is made **by hands**.
think: The restaurant's **lease** comes up next year with a big **rent rise**.
If rent goes up too much, the **place could close**.
do: Learn **bread** from the head baker every morning I can.
Keep using an **AI helper** to cost each loaf.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a little worry about the **lease**.
S0.quote: You can't learn bread from a video.
fieldNote: Elena's worry is a **lease renewal**, not technology.
Her real asset is a **mentor**, which she'd lose if the place closed.
She uses **AI occasionally** for costs while valuing handwork.

steps.text: Learn bread-making from the head baker each morning
Sell her loaves at the Saturday market
Save for the wedding and a future bakery
Use an AI helper to work out what each loaf costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines can't replace love in food. I'd also say, quietly, that people should learn the new tools if it helps their business. I'm not against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my cooking is safe for now, it's hands-on. But the owner's ordering and bookings would go on software, and maybe that saves Hearth and Grain enough to pay the higher rent. So it might even help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning bread, and I'd learn whatever booking or ordering system the restaurant uses, once the owner chooses one. I'd keep the market stall going. Mateo and I would carry on saving for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It could go either way, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it might even help. What would make you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the owner told me the place is safe because of it. I'd want to hear it from her, not guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plumbing is a good choice, because people will always need pipes fixed. Mateo laughs at me because I worry for both of us.

say: Whatever happens with software, machines can't replace **love in food**.
People should still **learn new tools** if it helps their business.
think: My **hands-on cooking** is safe for now.
Software for **bookings and ordering** might save enough to pay the higher rent.
do: Keep learning **bread** from the head baker.
Learn the restaurant's **booking system** once the owner picks one.
Keep the **market stall** going on Saturdays.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, because it could go either way.
S1.quote: Plumbing is a good choice, because people will always need pipes fixed.
fieldNote: She sees thinking-task software as possibly **saving the restaurant**.
Her **steady** style shows: she'd learn tools once chosen for her.
Her boyfriend's **trade** gives the household a sense of safety.

steps.text: Keep learning bread at Hearth and Grain
Learn the restaurant's new booking and ordering system
Keep the Saturday bread stall running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and people in power have let it happen. I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other. I'd say it with a lot of feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, 2028 hits the owner's paperwork, and by 2031 there's a robot that can do eggs and maybe even bread. Hearth and Grain would struggle against chains with robots. And robots that fix pipes in 2031 means Mateo too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married sooner and smaller, so we're a family whatever happens. I'd keep saving, aim for six months, and push the market stall so there's some income that's mine. I'd ask Agnes to teach me everything she can in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly for us as a family. I keep thinking about kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wanted them soon after the wedding. Now I'd think twice. I don't know what work they'd ever do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people still buy handmade bread from a stall if robots could make it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, the ones who care. Maybe it becomes a luxury, like hand-knitted jumpers. I'd be selling bread to the people who want a person to have made it.

say: It's **too fast**, and people in power let it happen.
**Families and churches** will have to carry each other.
think: By **2031** robots could do eggs and maybe bread, against cheaper chains.
Pipe-fixing robots mean my boyfriend's **plumbing** isn't safe either.
do: Marry **sooner and smaller** so we're a family whatever happens.
Save toward **six months** and grow the market stall income.
Ask the head baker to teach me **everything** in two years.
S2.quote: I'd be selling bread to the people who want a person to have made it.
fieldNote: She sees **both incomes** at risk once robots arrive in 2031.
Her answer is to **marry sooner**, not later, and lean on family.
She doubts having **children** in this picture.

steps.text: Marry sooner with a small church wedding
Save six months of household money
Grow the Saturday bread stall into a steady income
Rely on family and church if both incomes drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's prepare properly, with apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd say young people should learn real crafts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2034 for robots, I'd be thirty-five. That's enough time to learn bread properly and maybe open something small. But I'd be opening a bakery just before robot bakeries arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn everything from Agnes for three years. Keep the market stall and grow it to two days. Maybe open a tiny bakery around 2030, sell to people who want real bread, and see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but hopeful. There's a shape to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Opening a bakery just before robot bakeries. Would you still do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it's small and cheap to run. People still buy candles even though there's electricity. I'd be the candle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fund it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings, a small loan, and my dad's offered to help with the oven. Family helps family, that's how we do it.

say: There's time, so prepare with **apprenticeships**, not **handouts**.
Young people should learn **real crafts** like baking while the old hands can still teach them.
think: Robots arrive around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five, which is enough time to learn bread properly.
I might open a **bakery** just before **robot bakeries** arrive.
do: Learn everything from the head baker over **three years**.
Grow the market stall to **two days** a week.
feel: **Worried** but **hopeful**, because there's a shape to it.
S3.quote: People still buy candles even though there's electricity. I'd be the candle.
fieldNote: She'd still open a bakery, betting on **handmade value** as a niche.
Funding comes from **family**, matching her traditional outlook.
Five years lets her **build skill** before committing.

steps.text: Learn all of the head baker's bread methods over three years
Run the market stall two days a week
Open a tiny bakery around 2030 with savings and a loan
Accept her dad's help buying the bakery oven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody should panic. Use the time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, robots in 2039, I'd be forty, with my bakery maybe ten years old. That's a good run. And people who want real bread will still want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marry next year as planned, have children. Learn from Agnes, then open my bakery in four or five years. Mateo finishes his apprenticeship and works for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, mostly. A little unease about what my kids will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and their heart. A trade, or caring for people. I'd teach them bread either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use robots in your own bakery, by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Robots can do the mixing because it's heavy, but the shaping is the bit that's mine.

say: Use the decade to **build something** of your own, like a business or a trade.
think: By **2039** my bakery could be ten years old, which is a **good run**.
People who want **real bread** will still want it.
do: Marry **next year** and start a family.
Open my **bakery** in four or five years.
Support my boyfriend's plan to **work for himself**.
feel: **Content**, with a little unease about my **children's** future.
S4.quote: Robots can do the mixing because it's heavy, but the shaping is the bit that's mine.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **marry, have children** and open the bakery in order.
She'd use robots for **heavy mixing** but keep shaping by hand.
Her worry moves to her **children's** future work.

steps.text: Marry next year and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mateo and I would both be hit just as we start a family. What would help is real apprenticeships and small loans for people starting little businesses. Not handouts, a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who teach. Chef Agnes has forty years of bread in her hands. If nobody young learns from the old bakers before the robots come, forty years of knowledge is just gone.

headlineQuote: If nobody young learns from the old bakers before the robots come, forty years of knowledge is just gone.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old junior cook** at a busy brunch restaurant built around a wood **oven**.
She's learning bread from a **veteran baker** and dreams of her own **bakery**.
She's **traditional**, churchgoing and saving with her boyfriend, an apprentice **plumber**, to marry.
She uses AI **now and then** for costing, and adopts tools once they're **chosen** for her.
She moves from **uneasy** in most scenarios to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when both incomes look exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which hits both incomes just as they start a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: **Real apprenticeships** and **small loans** for people starting little businesses.
